Claim: Named family participants can hold different claims in resources; a household label does not specify those rights.
Nippur context: Private property agreements; precise houses not verified
Secondary interpretation: Analytical distinction based on the separate operative provisions.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Not every named seller or beneficiary holds the same kind or fraction of title.
Generalization limit: Attested arrangements, not a universal household property constitution.
Project relevance: Separates title, transfer, use, access, and benefit.

Claim: Women participate in house conveyances, but co-conveyance alone does not establish equal co-ownership.
Secondary interpretation: S04 examines co-sale clauses and competing explanations of women’s involvement.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Consent, retained interests, and ownership cannot be equated without the individual clauses.
Generalization limit: Legal participation is well attested; exact shares in these cases remain unresolved.
Project relevance: Prevents erasing women or assigning them unproven uniform rights.

Claim: A documented house partition was followed rapidly by three share purchases by one coheir.
Primary evidence: BE 6/2, 32–35; dates, dimensions, and neighbors; S01
Secondary interpretation: S04, p. 22 n. 45, identifies two brothers and a nephew as the sellers.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Poebel’s four-brothers shorthand is wrong; legal partition does not prove walls or separate residences.
Generalization limit: One securely linked sequence; no citywide consolidation rate or forced-sale motive.
Project relevance: Shows fragmentation and consolidation as historically successive transactions.

Claim: The consulted agreements vary between equal listed shares and a reserved eldest share before residual division.
Secondary interpretation: No universal rule inferred from this contrast.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Different instruments may cover different assets, prior gifts, or stages of inheritance.
Generalization limit: No fixed citywide eldest-share multiplier or uniform equal division.
Project relevance: Keeps inheritance arrangements contextual.

Claim: Division could distribute heterogeneous assets, including land, movable goods, resource entitlements, and enslaved persons, with balancing transfers.
Secondary interpretation: Portfolio description follows the texts; no standardized valuation model added.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Listed assets need not exhaust a household’s resources; some old furniture readings remain uncertain.
Generalization limit: Documented estates, not representative wealth or enslaved-person prices.
Project relevance: Distinguishes resource types and persons treated as property in the records.

Claim: Specified annual portions of temple-office entitlements could enter exchanges and inheritance divisions.
Secondary interpretation: S11 is a further specialist lead, abstract only; not the basis of detailed claims.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Transfer of an office portion is not ownership of the temple; actual performance and income are not observed.
Generalization limit: Particular transferable entitlements, not all temple offices or unrestricted marketability.
Project relevance: Separates income/service entitlement from buildings and land.

Claim: A partition could retain a common exit and leave other assets for later division.
Secondary interpretation: Legal/access reading, not an architectural reconstruction.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Shared access does not itself demonstrate co-residence; text does not say permanent indivisibility.
Generalization limit: One partially divided estate.
Project relevance: Shows continuing connections after a division.

Claim: A marriage agreement separately identifies the wife’s silver contribution and conditional return/forfeiture obligations.
Secondary interpretation: Terms read from the edition, with numerical clauses visually checked.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Not evidence that repudiation occurred; no comprehensive rule for all marriage property.
Generalization limit: One explicit agreement; daily control and actual enforcement unknown.
Project relevance: Distinguishes contribution, conditional claim, and available household cash.

Claim: Family maintenance obligations could be explicitly attached to continuing inheritance entitlement.
Secondary interpretation: Convergence concerns stipulated obligations, not demonstrated enforcement.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Forfeiture language is conditional; absence of receipts does not prove nonpayment.
Generalization limit: Two related types of agreement, not an obligation imposed on every relative.
Project relevance: Connects resource succession with ongoing support claims.

Claim: One support agreement restricts heirs’ alienation of fields during the beneficiary’s lifetime.
Nippur context: Bēltani, nadītu of Ninurta, and four brothers
Primary evidence: PBS 8/2, 116, tablet rev. 1–5 and envelope parallel; S02
Secondary interpretation: Interpreted narrowly as an express restriction within this arrangement.
Counterevidence/disagreement: No actual prohibited sale or forfeiture is documented; not proof of a universal family redemption right.
Generalization limit: This agreement only.
Project relevance: Shows that inheritance and unrestricted disposal are not identical.

Claim: The selected loan texts distinguish stated interest-bearing obligations from a text marked not bearing interest.
Secondary interpretation: No additional-interest wording is not assumed to prove zero total borrowing cost.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Principal may incorporate earlier charges; the interest-bearing text gives no rate.
Generalization limit: Terms of particular contracts, not citywide rates or prevalence.
Project relevance: Prevents applying one standard interest rule to all obligations.

Claim: An obligation could link different commodities or media at advance and settlement.
Primary evidence: PBS 8/2, 130: silver advance, barley return; BE 6/2, 16: grain with silver interest; no. 21: bricks; S01, S03
Secondary interpretation: Separate principal, interest, and return medium rather than one assumed cash balance.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Conversion rates, economic purpose, and discharge are not stated; no. 16 has uncertain provenance.
Generalization limit: Strong silver-to-barley case; grain/silver example remains qualified.
Project relevance: Distinguishes amounts owed from identical-resource replacement.

Claim: Named joint recipients can be bound together; this does not document liability of all household members.
Nippur context: Private loans; one uncertain Nippur attribution
Secondary interpretation: No automatic corporate-household debtor inferred.
Counterevidence/disagreement: No. 16 concerns a parent and son, not necessarily a mother and son; other kin and collateral are unrecorded.
Generalization limit: Joint wording does not establish the mechanics of joint-and-several liability.
Project relevance: Makes exposure personal and document-specific.

Claim: Cultivation and an annually assessed yield-share claim could be allocated through a lease rather than a permanent land sale.
Nippur context: Field described as that of Ninunu; Nippur contract
Secondary interpretation: Distinguishes lessor’s claim, lessee’s cultivation, and future crop share.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Actual harvest, occupancy, rent payment, and precise duration of the lease unknown.
Generalization limit: One lease; not the prevalence of share tenancy.
Project relevance: Separates land title/control from temporary use and revenue.

Claim: Future repayment clauses and an acknowledgment of money received are different kinds of evidence.
Nippur context: Legal text genres in the selected corpus
Primary evidence: BE 6/2, 65 versus PBS 8/2, 130 and BE 6/2, 15; S01, S03
Secondary interpretation: Analytical distinction between undertaking and recorded receipt.
Counterevidence/disagreement: The receipt concerns a house price, not a discharged loan; even a receipt is a legal representation.
Generalization limit: No repayment/default rate derived.
Project relevance: Prevents treating promised future behavior as an observed event.

Claim: A legal record narrates adjudication and an executed property settlement concerning earlier family transactions.
Nippur context: Nippur council; heirs of Iškur-rabi and Ududu
Primary evidence: BE 6/2, 10, especially final conveyance and non-claim clause; S01
Secondary interpretation: Read as recorded legal action, not independent observation of physical possession.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Not securely a debt foreclosure; early translation of built/unbuilt property needs checking.
Generalization limit: One litigation record, not an enforcement frequency or automatic inherited liability rule.
Project relevance: Supplies evidence beyond merely hypothetical sanctions.

Claim: Transfer of title documents could be accompanied by a future-claim undertaking.
Nippur context: Office-related title documents; precise findspot not verified
Secondary interpretation: Poebel infers institutional involvement from witnesses; that inference is not adopted as fact.
Counterevidence/disagreement: The text does not directly establish a temple sale or a third-party loan guarantee.
Generalization limit: Single document; scope of the undertaking needs modern re-edition.
Project relevance: Separates document custody, title claims, and responsibility for challenges.

Claim: A paternal house plot could be repurchased from the subsequent holder’s family.
Secondary interpretation: S04 questions certainty of matching the parcel to no. 38; S05 clarifies later family/custody.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Repurchase does not by itself prove mortgage, distress, or an enforceable right to force resale.
Generalization limit: Particular transaction, with an uncertain earlier deed match.
Project relevance: Shows family continuity through transfer without assuming inalienability.

Claim: A later dispute/waiver records an earlier house gift to a daughter and associated inheritance adjustments.
Period/date: Gift earlier than surviving Hammurabi 31/05 record
Secondary interpretation: S05, discussion pp. 9–13; primary edition S13 unavailable.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Retrospective record is not the gift instrument; full wording and compensation chain unverified.
Generalization limit: Scholarly mediated case, not a general gift or daughter-inheritance rule.
Project relevance: Identifies a gift pathway beyond sale and partition.

Claim: Subsistence provision could be followed by a litigated compensation claim affecting the recipient’s heirs.
Primary evidence: OECT 8, 11 = MC 3, 31, original not directly read
Secondary interpretation: S05 reports prebend compensation for grain/food supplied to Ibbi-Enlil.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Contractual basis, exact scope, and any adoptive relation must not be assumed; not a general inherited-debt rule.
Generalization limit: Mediated single case awaiting primary recheck.
Project relevance: Adds a bounded example of intergenerational economic exposure.

Claim: Reported excavated loans name a deity or a temple-linked source of silver, but the available contexts do not prove residence or a temple banking system.
Nippur context: Reported TA fill and disturbed TB contexts
Secondary interpretation: S08 selected indexed excerpt only; S07 full book inaccessible.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Fund ownership, lender’s role, rate period, and locus association need direct verification.
Generalization limit: Provisional retrieval leads, not a basis for institutional prevalence or standardized interest rates.
Project relevance: Preserves institution/private connections without conflating them.

Claim: This return does not establish a securely checked actual Nippur third-party loan guarantee or a collateral-enforcement sequence.
Period/date: Old Babylonian Nippur; didactic corpus kept separate
Nippur context: Access/sampling boundary, not a historical absence claim
Primary evidence: Selected actual loans S01, S03; no matched enforcement documents located within this return
Secondary interpretation: S09 school-text abstract; S14 lexical entry. Neither supplies an executed guarantee.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Other unconsulted contracts may supply such cases; keyword/OCR absence is not proof.
Generalization limit: HIGH for the stated research boundary, not for absence of ancient practices.
Project relevance: Keeps security and guaranty as open evidence questions.

Claim: A prosopographic dossier and a physically verified archive are not identical evidentiary objects.
Period/date: Old Babylonian family dossier; especially Samsu-iluna 29
Primary evidence: BE 6/2, 64 names his family after his death; S01
Secondary interpretation: S05 revises archive attribution and genealogical connections.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Same names, retrospective mentions, and later deeds can have different documentary custodians.
Generalization limit: Methodological conclusion; no exhaustive reconstruction of one original room archive.
Project relevance: Prevents equating property history, family identity, and co-residence.

Claim: The selected asset records permit case-level comparison but not representative household wealth estimates.
Period/date: Selected Old Babylonian regnal contexts, not the whole 1900–1600 BCE interval
Nippur context: Surviving edited legal cases and mediated family texts
Primary evidence: S01–S03 show selected transactions, not a census or complete estate accounts
Secondary interpretation: S04–S06 inform survival/publication/selection limits.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Unrecorded and undivided resources, missing records, and selection can change apparent portfolios.
Generalization limit: HIGH for inferential limit; no citywide wealth distribution estimated.
Project relevance: Blocks unsupported household classes, market prices, and prevalence claims.

Claim: One hire agreement distinguishes a father contracting, a son whose labor is hired, and a recipient of that labor.
Nippur context: Nabi-Šamaš and Iddin-Ištar; no identity merge across dossiers
Secondary interpretation: Used only for contracting/resource relations, not full labor-status analysis.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Age, consent, residence, and free/slave status are not determined here.
Generalization limit: Single agreement; no automatic household pooling of the wage claim.
Project relevance: Keeps person, contracting authority, and economic benefit distinct.
